claim: Kainate receptors (KARs) are L-glutamate-gated ion channels that regulate synaptic transmission and modulate neuronal circuits.
source: Kainate receptors (KARs) are L-glutamate-gated ion channels that regulate synaptic transmission and modulate neuronal circuits.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that describes the basic function of KARs, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: KARs have strict assembly rules and primarily function as heteromeric receptors in the brain.
source: KARs have strict assembly rules and primarily function as heteromeric receptors in the brain.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section referencing prior work (Herb et al., 1992; Petralia et al., 1994).

claim: The GluK2/GluK5 heteromer assembles with two copies of each subunit.
source: The receptor assembles with two copies of each subunit, ligand binding domains arranged as two heterodimers and GluK5 subunits proximal to the channel.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis presented in the manuscript, including Figure 1 and glycosylation site analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: In the GluK2/GluK5 heteromer, ligand binding domains are arranged as two heterodimers.
source: The receptor assembles with two copies of each subunit, ligand binding domains arranged as two heterodimers and GluK5 subunits proximal to the channel.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the LBD layer shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: GluK5 subunits are positioned proximal to the channel in the GluK2/GluK5 heteromer.
source: The receptor assembles with two copies of each subunit, ligand binding domains arranged as two heterodimers and GluK5 subunits proximal to the channel.
evidence: This is demonstrated by glycosylation site analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 8 showing GluK5 in A/C positions.

claim: During desensitization, GluK2, but not GluK5, subunits undergo major structural rearrangements to facilitate channel closure.
source: Strikingly, during desensitization, GluK2, but not GluK5, subunits undergo major structural rearrangements to facilitate channel closure.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of antagonist-bound and desensitized structures shown in Figures 4 and 5, demonstrating differential conformational changes.

claim: The large conformational differences between antagonist-bound and desensitized states are mediated by the linkers connecting the pore helices to the ligand binding domains.
source: We show how the large conformational differences between antagonist-bound and desensitized states are mediated by the linkers connecting the pore helices to the ligand binding domains.
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural analysis in Figure 5 showing M3-S2 linker conformational changes.

claim: Ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs) respond to the neurotransmitter L-glutamate (L-Glu) to mediate the majority of fast excitatory synaptic transmission in the human brain.
source: Ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs) respond to the neurotransmitter L-glutamate (L-Glu) to mediate the majority of fast excitatory synaptic transmission in the human brain (Dingledine et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dingledine et al., 1999, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: iGluRs have been implicated in major pathological brain conditions including depression, schizophrenia, stroke, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.
source: This central role has implicated iGluRs in major pathological brain conditions including depression, schizophrenia, stroke, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease (Bowie, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bowie, 2008.

claim: The iGluR family has three subtypes termed kainate receptors (KARs), α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPARs), and N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs).
source: The iGluR family has three subtypes termed kainate receptors (KARs), α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPARs), and N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) (Traynelis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation to Traynelis et al., 2010.

claim: KARs are expressed throughout the central nervous system and act post-synaptically in depolarization and modulation of membrane excitability.
source: KARs are expressed throughout the central nervous system and act post-synaptically in depolarization and modulation of membrane excitability, and pre-synaptically to regulate excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitter release (Contractor et al., 2011; Lerma and Marques, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Contractor et al., 2011 and Lerma and Marques, 2013.

claim: KARs act pre-synaptically to regulate excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitter release.
source: KARs are expressed throughout the central nervous system and act post-synaptically in depolarization and modulation of membrane excitability, and pre-synaptically to regulate excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitter release (Contractor et al., 2011; Lerma and Marques, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Contractor et al., 2011 and Lerma and Marques, 2013.

claim: KARs play a role in pain perception, epilepsy, and mood disorders.
source: Their role in pain perception, epilepsy, and mood disorders has also made KARs important targets of small-molecule antagonist and modulator development (Contractor et al., 2011; Larsen et al., 2017; Møllerud et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Contractor et al., 2011; Larsen et al., 2017; Møllerud et al., 2017.

claim: KARs are tetramers that assemble with four identical subunits (homomers) or mixtures of different subunits (heteromers).
source: KARs are tetramers that assemble with four identical subunits (homomers) or mixtures of different subunits (heteromers).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by subsequent citations in the text.

claim: Each KAR subunit has a modular three-layer design with an amino terminal domain (ATD), ligand binding domain (LBD), and transmembrane domain (TMD) which forms part of a common pore.
source: Each subunit has a modular three-layer design with an amino terminal domain (ATD), ligand binding domain (LBD), and transmembrane domain (TMD) which forms part of a common pore (Traynelis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Traynelis et al., 2010 and represents established structural knowledge.

claim: KAR tetramers have variable symmetry among their three domain layers.
source: The tetramers have variable symmetry among their three domain layers (Meyerson et al., 2016), a feature that is also found in AMPARs and NMDARs (Zhu and Gouaux, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Meyerson et al., 2016 and Zhu and Gouaux, 2017.

claim: Variable symmetry among domain layers is a feature also found in AMPARs and NMDARs.
source: The tetramers have variable symmetry among their three domain layers (Meyerson et al., 2016), a feature that is also found in AMPARs and NMDARs (Zhu and Gouaux, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhu and Gouaux, 2017.

claim: KAR tetramers are generated from a pool of five subunits.
source: KAR tetramers are generated from a pool of five subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: GluK1, GluK2, and GluK3 subunits can form functional homomers.
source: GluK1, GluK2, and GluK3 subunits can form functional homomers (Cui and Mayer, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cui and Mayer, 1999.

claim: GluK4 and GluK5 cannot form functional channels on their own and are obliged to co-assemble with GluK1, GluK2, or GluK3.
source: GluK4 and GluK5 cannot form functional channels on their own and are obliged to co-assemble with GluK1, GluK2, or GluK3 (Herb et al., 1992; Werner et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Herb et al., 1992 and Werner et al., 1991.

claim: GluK4-5 have higher L-Glu affinity than GluK1-3.
source: GluK4-5 also have higher L-Glu affinity (Herb et al., 1992) and thus a lower activation threshold than GluK1-3 (Barberis et al., 2008; Fisher and Mott, 2011; Mott et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Herb et al., 1992; Barberis et al., 2008; Fisher and Mott, 2011; Mott et al., 2010.

claim: GluK4-5 have a lower activation threshold than GluK1-3.
source: GluK4-5 also have higher L-Glu affinity (Herb et al., 1992) and thus a lower activation threshold than GluK1-3 (Barberis et al., 2008; Fisher and Mott, 2011; Mott et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barberis et al., 2008; Fisher and Mott, 2011; Mott et al., 2010.

claim: Heteromers containing GluK5 subunits show enhanced permeation to polyamine pore blockers.
source: Heteromers containing GluK5 subunits show enhanced permeation to polyamine pore blockers (Brown et al., 2016), distinct pharmacological properties (Herb et al., 1992; Swanson et al., 2002), and are endowed with slower deactivation kinetics (Barberis et al., 2008) which is proposed as central to their role in integrating synaptic signals (Frerking and Ohliger-Frerking, 2002; Lerma and Marques, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brown et al., 2016.

claim: Heteromers containing GluK5 subunits have distinct pharmacological properties.
source: Heteromers containing GluK5 subunits show enhanced permeation to polyamine pore blockers (Brown et al., 2016), distinct pharmacological properties (Herb et al., 1992; Swanson et al., 2002), and are endowed with slower deactivation kinetics (Barberis et al., 2008) which is proposed as central to their role in integrating synaptic signals (Frerking and Ohliger-Frerking, 2002; Lerma and Marques, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Herb et al., 1992 and Swanson et al., 2002.

claim: Heteromers containing GluK5 subunits are endowed with slower deactivation kinetics.
source: Heteromers containing GluK5 subunits show enhanced permeation to polyamine pore blockers (Brown et al., 2016), distinct pharmacological properties (Herb et al., 1992; Swanson et al., 2002), and are endowed with slower deactivation kinetics (Barberis et al., 2008) which is proposed as central to their role in integrating synaptic signals (Frerking and Ohliger-Frerking, 2002; Lerma and Marques, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Barberis et al., 2008.

claim: Slower deactivation kinetics of GluK5-containing heteromers is proposed as central to their role in integrating synaptic signals.
source: Heteromers containing GluK5 subunits show enhanced permeation to polyamine pore blockers (Brown et al., 2016), distinct pharmacological properties (Herb et al., 1992; Swanson et al., 2002), and are endowed with slower deactivation kinetics (Barberis et al., 2008) which is proposed as central to their role in integrating synaptic signals (Frerking and Ohliger-Frerking, 2002; Lerma and Marques, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Frerking and Ohliger-Frerking, 2002 and Lerma and Marques, 2013.

claim: Heteromers are thought to be the major KAR class in the brain.
source: Consequently homomers and heteromers occupy different functional niches in the brain, with heteromers thought to be the major KAR class (Herb et al., 1992; Petralia et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Herb et al., 1992 and Petralia et al., 1994.

claim: Receptors containing either GluK4 or GluK5 are specifically linked to diseases such as depression, epilepsy, autism, and schizophrenia.
source: Receptors containing either GluK4 or GluK5 are also specifically linked to diseases such as depression (Catches et al., 2012), epilepsy (Das et al., 2012), autism (Aller et al., 2015), and schizophrenia (Greenwood et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Catches et al., 2012; Das et al., 2012; Aller et al., 2015; and Greenwood et al., 2016.

claim: No KAR heteromer structure has been reported prior to this work.
source: Despite their significance, no KAR heteromer structure has been reported, which presents a major knowledge gap made more salient by recently reported structures of NMDAR (Karakas and Furukawa, 2014; Lee et al., 2014; Lü et al., 2017) and AMPAR heteromers (Herguedas et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work, supported by citations to existing NMDAR and AMPAR heteromer structures.

claim: L-Glu binding triggers the receptor to enter an active state with an open channel which allows cations to cross the membrane.
source: L-Glu binding triggers the receptor to enter an active state with an open channel which allows cations to cross the membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ligand-gated ion channel function.

claim: The channel closes again if L-Glu is rapidly removed (deactivation) or if L-Glu exposure is sustained (desensitization).
source: The channel closes again if L-Glu is rapidly removed (deactivation) or if L-Glu exposure is sustained (desensitization) (Barberis et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Barberis et al., 2008.

claim: Desensitized GluK2 and GluK3 homomers feature a 'desensitization ring' motif.
source: The desensitized structures revealed that KAR homomers feature a 'desensitization ring' motif which is proposed to facilitate channel closure and account for their slow recovery from desensitization (Meyerson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meyerson et al., 2016.

claim: The desensitization ring motif is proposed to facilitate channel closure and account for slow recovery from desensitization in KAR homomers.
source: The desensitized structures revealed that KAR homomers feature a 'desensitization ring' motif which is proposed to facilitate channel closure and account for their slow recovery from desensitization (Meyerson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meyerson et al., 2016.

claim: The desensitization ring motif has not been observed in AMPAR or NMDAR structures to date.
source: To date this motif has not been observed in AMPAR or NMDAR structures, raising the question of whether it is unique to KAR homomers or if KAR heteromers employ a similar desensitized structure.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of structural knowledge in the field.

claim: GluK2/GluK5 is proposed to be the major KAR in the brain.
source: Here, we report structures of the GluK2/GluK5 heteromer (GluK2/K5), proposed to be the major KAR in the brain (Herb et al., 1992; Petralia et al., 1994), in resting (apo), antagonist-bound (6-cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione [CNQX]), and agonist-bound (L-Glu) desensitized states.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Herb et al., 1992 and Petralia et al., 1994.

claim: The GluK2/K5 receptor has low expression levels in recombinant systems.
source: However, the GluK2/K5 receptor has low expression levels in recombinant systems (Hayes et al., 2003; Nasu-Nishimura et al., 2006; Reiner et al., 2012; Ren et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hayes et al., 2003; Nasu-Nishimura et al., 2006; Reiner et al., 2012; Ren et al., 2003.

claim: GluK2em and GluK5em can form functional heteromers with kinetic parameters comparable to wild-type receptors.
source: Taken together, GluK2/K5em heteromers exhibited the expected functional properties of rapid desensitization and relatively slow deactivation with kinetic parameters comparable to wild-type receptors (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Table 1.

claim: The GluK2/K5em-apo structure was resolved to 7.5 Å global resolution.
source: The data were processed using single particle analysis without symmetry applied and a structure of GluK2/K5em-apo was resolved to 7.5 Å global resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data processing results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Table 2.

claim: In the apo state, the four LBDs arrange as two pairs of dimers.
source: The four LBDs arrange as two pairs of dimers (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) which accord with a canonical model of a resting state structure (Dürr et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and citation to Dürr et al., 2014.

claim: The ATD layer in the apo state has a subtle 'tilt' away from the receptor central axis.
source: Lastly, the ATD layer has a subtle 'tilt' away from the receptor central axis and the linkers connecting the ATD and LBD layers were not resolved (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The ATD tilt in GluK2/K5 is similar to ATD tilts observed in AMPAR structures.
source: We note that this tilt is similar to ATD tilts observed in AMPAR structures solved by X-ray crystallography (Sobolevsky et al., 2009; Yelshanskaya et al., 2014) and cryo-EM (Nakagawa, 2019) and may reflect a general structural requirement for flexible ATD-LBD linkers to accommodate LBD movements during receptor gating.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sobolevsky et al., 2009; Yelshanskaya et al., 2014; and Nakagawa, 2019.

claim: The ATD tilt may reflect a general structural requirement for flexible ATD-LBD linkers to accommodate LBD movements during receptor gating.
source: We note that this tilt is similar to ATD tilts observed in AMPAR structures solved by X-ray crystallography (Sobolevsky et al., 2009; Yelshanskaya et al., 2014) and cryo-EM (Nakagawa, 2019) and may reflect a general structural requirement for flexible ATD-LBD linkers to accommodate LBD movements during receptor gating.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural observations and comparison to other iGluR structures.

claim: The GluK2/K5em-CNQX structure was refined to 5.3 Å resolution for the full-length receptor.
source: We prepared samples of GluK2/K5em with 1 mM CNQX, imaged with cryo-EM, processed the data using single particle analysis without symmetry applied, and refined a structure to 5.3 Å resolution (Figure 1—figure supplements 6 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data processing results shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 6 and 7 and Table 2.

claim: The ATD layer of GluK2/K5em-CNQX was refined to 3.6 Å resolution.
source: After subtracting the LBD and TMD layers from the particle set, we refined the ATD layer to 3.6 Å resolution, and then did the opposite by subtracting the ATD layer and refined the LBD-TMD assembly to 4.2 Å (Figure 1—figure supplements 6 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data processing results shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 6 and 7 and Table 2.

claim: The LBD-TMD assembly of GluK2/K5em-CNQX was refined to 4.2 Å resolution.
source: After subtracting the LBD and TMD layers from the particle set, we refined the ATD layer to 3.6 Å resolution, and then did the opposite by subtracting the ATD layer and refined the LBD-TMD assembly to 4.2 Å (Figure 1—figure supplements 6 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data processing results shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 6 and 7 and Table 2.

claim: The LBDs in GluK2/K5em-CNQX have 'open' binding clefts similar to antagonist-bound LBD structures.
source: Inspection of the conformational differences and the measured RMSD values showed clearly that the LBDs had 'open' binding clefts that were similar to the antagonist-bound LBD reference structure.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: GluK2em subunits form an interface between the two halves of the ATD layer (B/D positions).
source: This shows that GluK2em subunits form an interface between the two halves of the ATD layer (B/D positions), while the GluK5em ATDs heterodimerize with GluK2em ATDs which position them at the periphery of the ATD layer (A/C positions) (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is supported by glycosylation site analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: GluK5em ATDs heterodimerize with GluK2em ATDs and are positioned at the periphery of the ATD layer (A/C positions).
source: This shows that GluK2em subunits form an interface between the two halves of the ATD layer (B/D positions), while the GluK5em ATDs heterodimerize with GluK2em ATDs which position them at the periphery of the ATD layer (A/C positions) (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is supported by glycosylation site analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: GluK2/K5 receptors assemble with 2:2 stoichiometry.
source: Assigning the ATD identities allowed us to conclude that GluK2/K5 receptors assemble with 2:2 stoichiometry which is consistent with single molecule experiments (Litwin et al., 2020; Reiner et al., 2012), molecular dynamics simulation (Paramo et al., 2017), and an X-ray structure of isolated GluK2/K5 ATDs (PDB: 3QLV) (Kumar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by structural data from this study and citations to Litwin et al., 2020; Reiner et al., 2012; Paramo et al., 2017; and Kumar et al., 2011.

claim: In the full-length GluK2/K5 receptor, GluK2 and GluK5 LBDs assemble as two pairs of heterodimers.
source: Analysis of the GluK2/K5em-CNQX structure validates this hypothesis and shows that GluK2/K5 LBD heterodimers form with GluK5 in pore-proximal (A/C) positions and GluK2 in pore-distal (B/D) positions (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: In GluK2/K5 LBD heterodimers, GluK5 occupies pore-proximal (A/C) positions and GluK2 occupies pore-distal (B/D) positions.
source: Analysis of the GluK2/K5em-CNQX structure validates this hypothesis and shows that GluK2/K5 LBD heterodimers form with GluK5 in pore-proximal (A/C) positions and GluK2 in pore-distal (B/D) positions (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: The GluK2/K5 LBD layer is more compact than the GluK2 homomer or GluA1/A2 LBD layer.
source: From these measurements we conclude that the GluK2/K5 LBD layer is more compact than the GluK2 homomer or GluA1/A2 LBD layer, and in this respect is more akin to the GluN1b/N2B receptor.
evidence: This is supported by distance measurements between LBD centers of mass shown in Figure 2.

claim: The GluK2/K5 LBD layer is more akin to the GluN1b/N2B receptor in terms of compactness.
source: From these measurements we conclude that the GluK2/K5 LBD layer is more compact than the GluK2 homomer or GluA1/A2 LBD layer, and in this respect is more akin to the GluN1b/N2B receptor.
evidence: This is supported by distance measurements between LBD centers of mass shown in Figure 2.

claim: The GluK2/K5em-CNQX structure features three constrictions on the M3 helices at T652/T636, A656/A640, and T660/T644.
source: This analysis revealed three constrictions on the M3 helices at T652/T636, A656/A640, and T660/T644 (GluK2em/GluK5em subunits).
evidence: This is supported by pore profile analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The positions of pore constrictions in GluK2/K5 match those seen for the GluK2 homomer.
source: The positions of these constrictions match those seen for the GluK2 homomer (Meyerson et al., 2016) which reflects the strong sequence conservation for M3 helices within the KAR family.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to the GluK2 homomer structure (Meyerson et al., 2016) and sequence conservation.

claim: The GluK2/K5 pore is more similar to the AMPAR than the NMDAR.
source: These measurements highlight a similarity in pore structure for GluK2 and GluK2/K5em and also show the KAR heteromer pore is more similar to the AMPAR than the NMDAR.
evidence: This is supported by pore profile comparison shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The GluK2/K5em TMD maintains near fourfold rotational symmetry despite containing two different subunit types.
source: This near identity suggests that despite containing two different subunit types, the channel maintains near fourfold rotational symmetry.
evidence: This is supported by RMSD measurement of 1.5 Å between GluK2em and GluK5em subunit pairs shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The GluK2/K5em-L-Glu structure was resolved to 5.8 Å for the full-length receptor.
source: The data was processed using a similar approach to that used for the antagonist-bound dataset, and we first resolved the full-length L-Glu-bound receptor to 5.8 Å, then independently resolved the ATD layer (3.8 Å) and LBD-TMD assembly (4.3 Å) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data processing results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Table 2.

claim: The ATD layer of GluK2/K5em-L-Glu was resolved to 3.8 Å.
source: The data was processed using a similar approach to that used for the antagonist-bound dataset, and we first resolved the full-length L-Glu-bound receptor to 5.8 Å, then independently resolved the ATD layer (3.8 Å) and LBD-TMD assembly (4.3 Å) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data processing results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Table 2.

claim: The LBD-TMD assembly of GluK2/K5em-L-Glu was resolved to 4.3 Å.
source: The data was processed using a similar approach to that used for the antagonist-bound dataset, and we first resolved the full-length L-Glu-bound receptor to 5.8 Å, then independently resolved the ATD layer (3.8 Å) and LBD-TMD assembly (4.3 Å) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data processing results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Table 2.

claim: The LBDs in GluK2/K5em-L-Glu are similar to L-Glu-bound LBD crystal structures.
source: The structural alignments and the measured RMSD values showed unambiguously that the LBDs are similar to the L-Glu-bound LBD crystal structure.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5C.

claim: The LBD layer of GluK2/K5em-L-Glu shows rupture of both LBD dimer pairs.
source: The most striking feature of the GluK2/K5em-L-Glu structure is the LBD layer, which shows rupture of both LBD dimer pairs and exhibits an apparent fourfold symmetric subunit arrangement (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4.

claim: The LBD layer of GluK2/K5em-L-Glu exhibits an apparent fourfold symmetric subunit arrangement.
source: The most striking feature of the GluK2/K5em-L-Glu structure is the LBD layer, which shows rupture of both LBD dimer pairs and exhibits an apparent fourfold symmetric subunit arrangement (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4.

claim: The G helices of all four LBDs in GluK2/K5em-L-Glu come together in a staggered arrangement to render the layer twofold symmetric.
source: Although the LBD layer gives the impression of fourfold symmetry, close inspection shows that the G helices of all four LBDs come together in a staggered arrangement to render the layer twofold symmetric (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The LBD arrangement in desensitized GluK2/K5 is reminiscent of the 'desensitization ring' observed in the desensitized GluK2 homomer structure.
source: Critically, this arrangement is reminiscent of the 'desensitization ring' observed in the desensitized GluK2 homomer structure (Meyerson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to the GluK2 homomer structure shown in Figure 4 and citation to Meyerson et al., 2016.

claim: GluK5em G helices reside ~3 Å closer to each other across the twofold symmetry plane compared to analogous GluK2 subunits in the homomer.
source: Furthermore, close inspection shows GluK5em G helices reside ~3 Å closer to each other across the twofold symmetry plane of the LBD layer, compared to analogous GluK2 subunits in the homomer (Figure 4E,H).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4E and 4H.

claim: The closer positioning of GluK5em G helices produces a more compact desensitization ring in the heteromer.
source: This subtle difference has a geometric consequence of producing a more compact desensitization ring in the heteromer (Figure 4E,H, insets).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural measurements shown in Figure 4E and 4H.

claim: Relative to the CNQX-bound structure, the L-Glu-bound GluK5em LBDs (A/C positions) are turned in plane by ~18°.
source: The analysis showed that relative to the CNQX-bound structure, the L-Glu-bound GluK5em LBDs (A/C positions) are turned in plane by ~18°, while the GluK2em LBDs (B/D positions) are rotated by ~110° (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4.

claim: Relative to the CNQX-bound structure, the L-Glu-bound GluK2em LBDs (B/D positions) are rotated by ~110°.
source: The analysis showed that relative to the CNQX-bound structure, the L-Glu-bound GluK5em LBDs (A/C positions) are turned in plane by ~18°, while the GluK2em LBDs (B/D positions) are rotated by ~110° (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4.

claim: GluK5em LBDs pitch back by ~10° more than GluK2 partner subunits in the desensitized state.
source: Meanwhile, the GluK5em LBDs pitch back by ~10° more than GluK2 partner subunits (Figure 4F, inset), while both GluK2em and GluK5em show the same change in cleft closure (~20°) between their open-cleft (CNQX) and closed-cleft (L-Glu) states.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Both GluK2em and GluK5em show the same change in cleft closure (~20°) between their open-cleft (CNQX) and closed-cleft (L-Glu) states.
source: Meanwhile, the GluK5em LBDs pitch back by ~10° more than GluK2 partner subunits (Figure 4F, inset), while both GluK2em and GluK5em show the same change in cleft closure (~20°) between their open-cleft (CNQX) and closed-cleft (L-Glu) states.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: All four LBDs in the desensitized structure have closed clefts consistent with agonist binding.
source: Critically, this latter measurement confirms that while the resolution of the desensitized structure is not sufficient to resolve ligand density, all four LBDs have closed clefts consistent with agonist binding (Møllerud et al., 2017; Figure 1—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5C and citation to Møllerud et al., 2017.

claim: The M3 helices in both CNQX-bound and L-Glu-bound structures are similar with an RMSD of 2.8 Å.
source: The M3 helices (L631/L615 to M664/M648 for GluK2em/GluK5em) in both structures are similar with an RMSD of 2.8 Å.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: The similarity in M3 helices indicates that the LBD-TMD linkers alone accommodate the two distinct LBD layer configurations.
source: The similarity in M3 helices indicates that the LBD-TMD linkers alone accommodate the two distinct LBD layer configurations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural comparison showing similar M3 helices but different LBD arrangements.

claim: Residue E662 on the M3 helices of GluK2em is the key site where the antagonist-bound and agonist-bound chains diverge.
source: Through this calculation we identified residue E662 on the M3 helices of GluK2em as the key site where the antagonist-bound and agonist-bound chains diverge (Figure 5E, arrow).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: GluK5em (A/C) linker elevation does not differ significantly between antagonist-bound and desensitized conformations.
source: This vertical analysis revealed that GluK5em (A/C) linker elevation does not differ significantly between antagonist-bound and desensitized conformations.
evidence: This is supported by vertical position analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: For GluK2em (B/D) subunits, the M3-S2 linkers extend ~12 Å further from the membrane in the desensitized state.
source: Meanwhile, for GluK2em (B/D) subunits, the M3-S2 linkers extend ~12 Å further from the membrane in the desensitized state.
evidence: This is supported by vertical position analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The M3-S2 linkers on the GluK2 subunit are the core structural element that allows GluK2/K5 to adopt two significantly different LBD arrangements in the antagonist-bound and desensitized states.
source: This analysis yields the conclusion that the M3-S2 linkers on the GluK2 subunit are the core structural element that allows GluK2/K5 to adopt two significantly different LBD arrangements in the antagonist-bound and desensitized states.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: GluK5 is distinguished from GluK2 in that it has high L-Glu affinity and slow deactivation kinetics.
source: GluK5 is distinguished from GluK2 in that it has high L-Glu affinity and slow deactivation kinetics, which sustains non-desensitizing currents in GluK2/K5 heteromers (Barberis et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Barberis et al., 2008.

claim: At low neurotransmitter concentration, GluK2/K5 is activated by ligand binding to the GluK5 subunits without binding to GluK2 subunits.
source: Because of the high affinity of GluK5 for L-Glu, at low neurotransmitter concentration GluK2/K5 is activated by ligand binding to the GluK5 subunits without binding to GluK2 subunits (Fisher and Mott, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fisher and Mott, 2011.

claim: Desensitization in GluK2/K5 is triggered when GluK2 subunits are also bound by neurotransmitter.
source: Functional studies have found that desensitization is triggered when GluK2 subunits are also bound by neurotransmitter (Fisher and Fisher, 2014; Reiner and Isacoff, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fisher and Fisher, 2014 and Reiner and Isacoff, 2014.

claim: The desensitized GluK2/K5 structure suggests that it is the GluK2 subunits which undergo large conformational changes to facilitate channel closure during desensitization.
source: The desensitized GluK2/K5 structure helps rationalize this functional role for GluK2, suggesting that it is the GluK2 subunits which undergo large conformational changes to facilitate channel closure during desensitization (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The LBD layer of desensitized GluK2/K5 is organized with pseudo-fourfold symmetry.
source: This study shows that the LBD layer of desensitized GluK2/K5 is organized with pseudo-fourfold symmetry and with the four LBDs positioned such that their G helices are in a staggered arrangement near the central axis of the receptor (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The LBD configuration in desensitized GluK2/K5 is similar to that observed in desensitized GluK2 and GluK3.
source: This LBD configuration is similar to that observed in desensitized GluK2 (Figure 4H; Meyerson et al., 2016) and GluK3 (Kumari et al., 2019), which suggests the arrangement is a hallmark of desensitization in the KAR family.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to structures of desensitized GluK2 and GluK3, with citations to Meyerson et al., 2016 and Kumari et al., 2019.

claim: The desensitized LBD arrangement is a hallmark of desensitization in the KAR family.
source: This LBD configuration is similar to that observed in desensitized GluK2 (Figure 4H; Meyerson et al., 2016) and GluK3 (Kumari et al., 2019), which suggests the arrangement is a hallmark of desensitization in the KAR family.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of multiple KAR structures.

claim: Desensitization must involve reorganizing the LBD dimer interface to allow LBDs to remain bound to L-Glu while also closing the channel.
source: However, it is clear that desensitization must involve reorganizing the LBD dimer interface to allow LBDs to remain bound to L-Glu while also closing the channel (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Armstrong et al., 2006; Twomey and Sobolevsky, 2018; Zhu and Gouaux, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by functional data and citations to Armstrong et al., 2006; Twomey and Sobolevsky, 2018; Zhu and Gouaux, 2017.

claim: The E662 position at the top of the M3 helices on GluK2 may serve as a fixed point around which GluK2 LBDs and M3-S2 linkers rotate during desensitization.
source: Furthermore, the E662 position at the top of the M3 helices on GluK2 may serve as a fixed point around which GluK2 LBDs and M3-S2 linkers rotate during desensitization (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: KAR homomers are regulated by extracellular ions that bind to the LBDs.
source: Previous electrophysiology of KARs and X-ray crystallography of isolated LBDs have demonstrated that KAR homomers are regulated by extracellular ions that bind to the LBDs (Dawe et al., 2013; Plested and Mayer, 2007; Plested et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dawe et al., 2013; Plested and Mayer, 2007; Plested et al., 2008.

claim: The canonical view of ion-dependent gating in homomeric receptors is different in GluK2/K5 heteromers.
source: However, a recent molecular dynamics study suggests that the canonical view of ion-dependent gating in homomeric receptors (Dawe et al., 2013) is different in GluK2/K5 heteromers (Paramo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Paramo et al., 2017.

claim: Sodium stabilizes GluK2 homomers, with a weaker allosteric effect by lithium ions.
source: Specifically, while sodium stabilizes GluK2 homomers, with a weaker allosteric effect by lithium ions, the situation is reversed in GluK2/K5 heteromers where lithium potentiates the agonist response and prolongs the rate of desensitization.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Paramo et al., 2017 in the preceding sentence.

claim: In GluK2/K5 heteromers, lithium potentiates the agonist response and prolongs the rate of desensitization.
source: Specifically, while sodium stabilizes GluK2 homomers, with a weaker allosteric effect by lithium ions, the situation is reversed in GluK2/K5 heteromers where lithium potentiates the agonist response and prolongs the rate of desensitization.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Paramo et al., 2017 in the preceding sentence.

claim: After refining the full-length structures of CNQX-bound and L-Glu-bound GluK2/K5em, the resolutions of the ATD layer and the LBD-TMD assembly could be improved with local refinement.
source: It is notable that after refining the full-length structures of CNQX-bound and L-Glu-bound GluK2/K5em, we found that the resolutions of the ATD layer and the LBD-TMD assembly could be improved with local refinement (Figure 1—figure supplement 7, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ability to improve resolution with local refinement suggests some degree of relative mobility between the ATD and LBD-TMD regions permitted by the ATD-LBD linkers.
source: This suggests some degree of relative mobility between these regions permitted by the ATD-LBD linkers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that local refinement improved resolution.

claim: Close comparison showed no significant differences between the CNQX-bound and L-Glu-bound ATD layers.
source: However, close comparison showed no significant differences between the two ATD layers which is consistent with the idea that KAR ATDs are not involved in channel gating.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: KAR ATDs are not involved in channel gating.
source: However, close comparison showed no significant differences between the two ATD layers which is consistent with the idea that KAR ATDs are not involved in channel gating.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of structural differences between ATD layers in different functional states.

claim: KAR ATDs play a key role in subunit oligomerization during receptor biogenesis.
source: Rather, they are thought to play a key role in subunit oligomerization during receptor biogenesis (Kumar et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kumar et al., 2011 and Zhao et al., 2017.

claim: Despite extensive image classification, no evidence was found for GluK5 adopting alternative positions (i.e. B or D) in the receptor.
source: Despite this effort we did not find evidence that such particle subsets exist in the datasets.
evidence: This is based on extensive image classification analysis during data processing.

claim: Given the 10-fold excess of GluK5em versus GluK2em virus added during protein expression, GluK5 would be expected to adopt alternative positions if this were possible.
source: Importantly, given the 10-fold excess of GluK5em versus GluK2em virus added during protein expression, we would expect GluK5 to adopt alternative positions (i.e. B or D) if this were possible.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the expression conditions.

claim: GluK5 can only occupy the A/C positions in the GluK2/K5 heteromer.
source: That this does not happen led us to conclude that GluK5 can only occupy the A/C positions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lack of evidence for alternative arrangements despite favorable expression conditions.

claim: This work provides the first structures of the presumed major neuronal type of KAR.
source: This study marks a milestone in iGluR biology by providing the first structures of the presumed major neuronal type of KAR to accompany structures of the dominant forms of NMDARs and AMPARs.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the work in the context of the field.

claim: The structures answer long-standing questions about domain arrangements and orientations in GluK2/K5.
source: The structures answer long-standing questions about domain arrangements and orientations, and they lay a foundation for high-resolution studies of GluK2/K5 to fully illuminate its gating mechanism and coordination of small-molecule agonists, antagonists, and modulators (Jane et al., 2009; Larsen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the contribution of the work, supported by citations to Jane et al., 2009 and Larsen et al., 2017.

claim: The availability of molecular models for all iGluR family members now makes possible comparative structure-guided investigation across the iGluR family.
source: Together the availability of molecular models for all iGluR family members now makes possible comparative structure-guided investigation across the iGluR family and a framework for precision targeting of drugs to specific receptor subtypes.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader impact of having structures for all major iGluR types.
